content.text: "Linear" in linear regression means the prediction is a weighted sum of the features, not that the result is a straight line. Feed the same model
, and it fits curves with the same fast, interpretable training. Before switching algorithms because the data bends, try changing the features.
An analyst plots a city's daily electricity demand against temperature and sees a U: demand climbs on cold days for heating and on hot days for cooling. She fits

, gets a slope of almost zero and a cross-validated score below zero, and writes in the ticket: "Linear regression can't do curves, moving to a neural network." The model wasn't the problem. Its inputs were.
Many developers believe linear regression can only model straight-line relationships, so curved data always needs a different algorithm. The belief is easy to come by:

items.text: The name says "linear", and every introduction shows the same picture: a straight line through a cloud of points.
really does draw a straight line. That first experience sticks.
looks like a straight line (or a flat plane) in the inputs.

content.text: All three observations are true for the raw features. The mistake is assuming the model must use the raw features. Linear regression is linear in its weights, and you choose what those weights multiply.
The scikit-learn user guide defines linear models as methods where the target is expected to be a linear combination of the features. The word that matters is
: they can be anything you compute from the raw inputs.
and build new features from them:
. A model that learns one weight per new feature can fit a curved surface, yet the user guide points out that this is still a linear model: the prediction is linear in
, so the same solver fits it. Nothing about the algorithm changes; it just works in a bigger feature space.
adds powers and products of your columns.
splits each feature's range into pieces joined at points called knots and adds a smooth curve segment per piece.
Here's the electricity story with synthetic data. Demand follows a U centered on 18 °C, plus noise. The score is
: 1.0 is a perfect fit, 0.0 is what you'd get by always predicting the average, and below zero is worse than that.

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
temp = rng.uniform(-5, 40, 500).reshape(-1, 1)  # daily temperature in C
# Demand rises on cold days (heating) and on hot days (cooling)
demand = 0.08 * (temp[:, 0] - 18) ** 2 + 50 + rng.normal(0, 3, 500)

line = LinearRegression().fit(temp, demand)
print(f"slope {line.coef_[0]:.4f}")  # slope -0.0019
r2 = cross_val_score(LinearRegression(), temp, demand, cv=5).mean()
print(f"R2 {r2:.3f}")  # R2 -0.034

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures, SplineTransformer

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
temp = rng.uniform(-5, 40, 500).reshape(-1, 1)  # daily temperature in C
demand = 0.08 * (temp[:, 0] - 18) ** 2 + 50 + rng.normal(0, 3, 500)

# Same LinearRegression, new features: temp and temp**2, or spline pieces
poly = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(degree=2), LinearRegression())
spline = make_pipeline(SplineTransformer(), LinearRegression())
forest = RandomForestRegressor(random_state=0)  # a "different algorithm"
for name, model in [("degree 2", poly), ("spline", spline), ("forest", forest)]:
    r2 = cross_val_score(model, temp, demand, cv=5).mean()
    print(f"{name:<9}R2 {r2:.3f}")  # 0.949, 0.949, 0.926
print(poly.fit(temp, demand)[-1].coef_.round(3))  # [ 0.    -2.909  0.081]

content.text: The straight line prints a slope of -0.0019 and an R² of -0.034. Read literally, it says temperature doesn't affect demand, when temperature drives almost all of it. A line through a symmetric U is nearly flat, so its errors cancel out into "no effect".

reaches 0.949. The cubic spline (scikit-learn's defaults: 5 knots, degree 3) matches it. A random forest, the "different algorithm", scores 0.926 on this data: switching models wasn't needed to fix the curve. And the weights stay readable. The data was generated from

Both are features for a linear model, but they behave differently at the edges. The preprocessing guide warns that polynomials oscillate near the boundaries, worse as the degree grows (Runge's phenomenon), and the interpolation example calls high powers particularly dangerous for extrapolating beyond the fitted range. Splines stay smooth, keep a low degree (usually 3), and let you control what happens past the last knot: by default they continue with a constant. One difference to remember:

content.text: Plot the residuals (actual minus predicted) against each feature. If they form a curve instead of a shapeless band, the model is missing a transform of that feature. Start with

blocks.title: Watch the edges of your data

content.text: High-degree polynomial features shoot up or down outside the range they were trained on, so a forecast for an unusually hot day can be far off. Polynomial features also multiply in number: degree 3 on 30 columns produces 5,456 features. With many inputs, prefer splines per feature, add regularization such as
, or let a tree-based model find interactions.
How to apply it in your project
Plot the target against each important feature, or the residuals of your current linear model. A clear bend points to a feature problem, not an algorithm problem.

items.title: Check what happens past your data

content.text: Predict a few values just beyond your training range. If the curve shoots off, prefer splines or clip inputs to the range you trained on.

items.text: Linear regression is linear in its weights, not in the raw inputs.
Powers, products and spline pieces of a feature let the same model fit curves and stay interpretable.
A flat line through U-shaped data hides a strong effect; plot before concluding "no relationship".
Prefer low-degree splines over high-degree polynomials, and check behavior outside the training range.
